initial_review.original_reference_answer: In Tang et al.'s joint crowd-evacuation and vehicle-scheduling MILP, demand switching is modelled by the continuous, non-negative decision variable pi_i^{l,l'}(k): the number of passengers whose preferred line is l who are reassigned to line l' at source cell i during interval k. Switching is allowed only at source cells (origin zones), i.e. before passengers start walking through the hub network, and only among shared transportation lines L_S (shuttle, taxi, subway, bus); private-car passengers (mode 5) cannot switch, and nobody switches after boarding. How many may switch is governed by two constraints: Eq. (8) caps the total switched from l to l' at source cell i over the horizon at rho^{l,l'} times the total demand for l at that cell (rho^{l,l'} in [0,1] is a parameter for the maximum switchable proportion, lower when lines overlap less or differ more in comfort/price), and Eq. (9) keeps the number switched away from l in each interval at most the original demand D_i^l(k). The variables enter the source-cell flow conservation Eq. (5) (demand for line l at the source cell becomes D_i^l(k) plus inflows switched to l minus outflows switched away from l) and the line-level completion constraint Eq. (7) (all redistributed demand of each line must eventually board that line's vehicles). The objective term Z3 adds a per-passenger switching cost c_D^{l,l'} times pi (interpretable as a hub subsidy), so switching is penalised and traded off against travel-time and vehicle-operation costs. In the solution algorithm pi is a continuous subproblem variable, and the same switching constraints reappear in the time-expanded reformulation (B.2), (B.7), (B.8).
initial_review.question: In the paper on jointly optimizing crowd evacuation and vehicle scheduling at multimodal transportation hubs, how is the demand-switching strategy between transport modes represented in the mixed-integer linear programming model? I'd like to know which decision variables and constraints govern when and how many passengers can switch from one mode to another.

change_log.after: Zhao et al. treat the measured skin conductance response (SCR) amplitude P as a proxy for the social repulsive force divided by a unit conversion factor alpha (N/uS), i.e. P = F_ij^rep / alpha. For each pass of the moving participant through the stationary crowd they build one sample point: the SCR amplitude of that event, extracted automatically with the Autonomate method (event-related window, latency 0.5-4 s, onset-to-peak <= 4 s, a minimum amplitude threshold of 0.02 uS (the text says above the threshold); only the first two samples per participant to limit habituation), paired with the interpersonal distance r_ij - d_ij taken at the minimum centre distance d_ij to the nearest stationary pedestrian (r_ij uses the lateral body width l_i cos(theta_i) to account for body twisting). These P versus r_ij - d_ij data (range -0.04 to 0.10 m) are fitted with two functional forms: the classical exponential P = A~_i e^{(r_ij-d_ij)/B_i} (Eq. 2, A~_i in uS) and a proposed logistic P = SCR_max / (1 + e^{-k_0 (r_ij - d_ij - s_0)}) (Eq. 3). The coefficients (A~_i, B_i; SCR_max, s_0, k_0) are estimated by generalized least squares separately for the walking, running and blind experiments and reported in Table 1 (e.g. walking logistic SCR_max = 0.283 uS, s_0 = 0.007 m, k_0 = 95.069 m^-1; exponential A~_i = 0.138 uS, B_i = 0.084 m); the logistic form fits better (R2 0.578/0.538/0.603 vs 0.392/0.394/0.475). The amplitude parameters A~_i and SCR_max are in uS, B_i and s_0 are in m, and k_0 is in m^-1. In the modified social force model the SCR response function's output is multiplied by alpha, set as a 'reasonable estimate' of 2.10 x 10^3 N/uS, to give the repulsive force magnitude (Eq. 7). Equivalently, alpha rescales the amplitude, not the distance parameters B_i and s_0 or the slope parameter k_0. Face-to-face/face-to-back orientation enters only through mean SCR comparisons and, in validation simulations, a smaller face-to-back SCR_max (0.085 uS) whose derivation is not detailed.

initial_review.original_reference_answer: Zhao et al. treat the measured skin conductance response (SCR) amplitude P as a proxy for the social repulsive force divided by a unit conversion factor alpha (N/uS), i.e. P = F_ij^rep / alpha. For each pass of the moving participant through the stationary crowd they build one sample point: the SCR amplitude of that event, extracted automatically with the Autonomate method (event-related window, latency 0.5-4 s, onset-to-peak <= 4 s, amplitude >= 0.02 uS; only the first two samples per participant to limit habituation), paired with the interpersonal distance r_ij - d_ij taken at the minimum centre distance d_ij to the nearest stationary pedestrian (r_ij uses the lateral body width l_i cos(theta_i) to account for body twisting). These P versus r_ij - d_ij data (range -0.04 to 0.10 m) are fitted with two functional forms: the classical exponential P = A~_i e^{(r_ij-d_ij)/B_i} (Eq. 2, A~_i in uS) and a proposed logistic P = SCR_max / (1 + e^{-k_0 (r_ij - d_ij - s_0)}) (Eq. 3). The coefficients (A~_i, B_i; SCR_max, s_0, k_0) are estimated by generalized least squares separately for the walking, running and blind experiments and reported in Table 1 (e.g. walking logistic SCR_max = 0.283 uS, s_0 = 0.007 m, k_0 = 95.069 m^-1; exponential A~_i = 0.138 uS, B_i = 0.084 m); the logistic form fits better (R2 0.578/0.538/0.603 vs 0.392/0.394/0.475). In the modified social force model these SCR-scale coefficients are multiplied by alpha, set as a 'reasonable estimate' of 2.10 x 10^3 N/uS, to give the force (Eq. 7). Face-to-face/face-to-back orientation enters only through mean SCR comparisons and, in validation simulations, a smaller face-to-back SCR_max (0.085 uS) whose derivation is not detailed.

initial_review.original_reference_answer: Both schemes retain density rho and potential phi. ev-PINN adds speed u and cost c as network outputs and adds algebraic consistency residuals f6=u-U(rho,x,y) and f7=c-C(rho,x,y); it retains the Eikonal residual f1 and the substituted conservation residual f2, with the latter still involving second spatial derivatives. ro-PINN instead adds flow components qx and qy. Its residual set is f1 (Eikonal), f3=rho_t+(qx)_x+(qy)_y (conservation) and f4/f5 (consistency of predicted flows with the potential-gradient flux relation), using first derivatives. The paper lists the combined PDE residual terms as f1+f2+f6+f7 for ev-PINN and f1+f3+f4+f5 for ro-PINN. It defines a squared residual collocation loss in Eq9, boundary-condition losses and initial-condition losses, and combines them as Jloss=alpha Jres+beta Jbc+Jinit. Boundary penalties enforce inlet flow, wall flow and outlet potential; transient initial penalties constrain density and both flow components. Two publication caveats should be preserved: Eq17 prints phi_x in the qy residual although the defining qy relation Eq7 uses phi_y; and the later residual-sum shorthand should not be read as an unqualified new unsquared training objective overriding Eq9. Report the printed construction and inconsistency rather than silently correcting the paper or inventing an implementation.

initial_review.original_reference_answer: Quiescent behavior is the phase in which a pedestrian speed is below 0.1 m/s, interpreted as a stop phase. Quiescent time tq is the duration of that low-speed state, rather than the interval between consecutive pedestrians crossing the entrance or the entire evacuation time. The authors extract trajectories with PeTrack, smooth them by a mean filter to reduce head/body sway, and conduct subsequent analyses using the smoothed trajectories together with video. Speed is calculated from coordinate changes; applying the threshold identifies the low-speed phase and its elapsed duration. The paper does not specify a separate minimum-dwell rule or gap-merging convention, so these should not be invented. Its smoothing description says about one second/50 frames and specifies Delta t=24 frames; that wording need not be silently converted into an exact 50-sample implementation.

initial_review.original_reference_answer: The comfort indicator is the trajectory-average local density experienced by pedestrian j in experiment i. At each time the local density rho_i,j(t) is computed by a Voronoi diagram; the paper writes rho_i,j=sum from t_s to t_e of rho_i,j(t), divided by (t_e-t_s). It describes this as the overall walking-surroundings indicator. It is a density-based proxy, not a questionnaire rating, and the printed expression should be retained rather than silently adding a timestep or changing the endpoint normalization. For reproducing it from discrete samples, sampling/normalization conventions need to be kept consistent with the paper; this question does not require inferring unreported code.

initial_review.original_reference_answer: The strategic layer separates leader placement from dynamic exit selection. Placement minimizes leader number M=sum_i X_i, subject to coverage of each cell containing pedestrians unable to find exits: sum_i X_i Z_i,j>=1, with X_i and Z_i,j binary (location and coverage indicators). It is not an objective directly minimizing evacuation time or hazard probability. Exit selection chooses the smallest dynamic weight W_lk=D_lk+delta P_lk/B_k. Risk is represented by Euclidean distance D_lk to the exit (longer means greater risk), while congestion is the count P_lk of pedestrians closer to exit k than the leader, normalized by exit width B_k. From the CTPF distribution, cells not guided by leader l contribute rho_i A_i when closer, and half that occupancy when equally distant. Thus risk and congestion are modeling proxies in the exit-choice score; delta controls the congestion contribution. initial_review.original_reference_answer: A binary attention state evolves as a first-order Markov chain. Initiation and continuation/termination probabilities use polynomial logistic functions of angular separation (shop visual size) and observation angle (walking direction versus shop entrance midpoint); next state is a Bernoulli sample. A simulation-only small angular-separation cutoff forces no attention. While attending, desired speed is neutral speed scaled by min(ideal/current angular speed,1); ideal angular speed is sampled once per pedestrian and current angular speed concerns the display midpoint. Without attention neutral speed applies. This dynamic desired speed enters the SFM goal force, slowing near displays rather than adding a shop-attraction force.

change_log.after: In order to deal efficiently with high statistics data and prevent unbounded cells, we consider here an approach that builds on bounding individual areas from the start, echoing the concept of personal space. The personal space is defined as the space a walking pedestrian tries to maintain around the body. While it is understood to be elliptical (axes: 2 m in longitudinal and 0.5 m in lateral direction according to Gérin-Lajoie et al. (2008)), we approximate the individual personal space of the pedestrian, i, as a circular region with radius R= 0.75 m and area πR2 = 1.86 m2. In level-of-service terms, this is at the interface between level A (free-flow) and B (slightly restricted flow), as defined by Fruin (1971). We compute the instantaneous density as the ratio between the number of observed pedestrians and the union of all the personal spaces, [...] where Oregionindicates the observation region, that is used as outer limit of the personal areas.

change_log.after: The corpus offers context-dependent evidence. In a computer-based virtual evacuation, participants preferred a wider exit; making the shorter route visible did not significantly increase shortest-route choice. Route choices and defined direction changes were recorded and analyzed using generalized linear models. This experiment was not a direct test of real pedestrian dynamics. In actual-incident videos, staff guidance was associated with fewer delayed responses. Communications and risk behaviors were coded from videos and assessed with chi-square and logistic analyses; these are associations, not causal intervention effects. If the alarm finding is reported, the increased delay association was significant in the unadjusted analysis, while the adjusted alarm coefficient was not significant (p=0.25). Either study provides a complete cue-response and measurement example under its own conditions.
change_log.before: The corpus gives context-dependent responses to wayfinding and communication cues. In a computer-based virtual evacuation, participants favored a wider exit; making the shorter route visible did not significantly change shortest-route choice. Logged choices and direction changes were analyzed by binomial GLMs and route-choice model comparisons; dynamic queues mattered. This is not a direct real-world emergency test. In actual-incident videos, staff guiding people to exits was associated with fewer delayed responses; alarm alone was associated with more delay. Video coding recorded communications and risk behaviors, with chi-square/logistic analyses; associations are not causal intervention effects. Normal-condition desktop VR signage work is related evidence, not emergency-sign compliance calibration.

change_log.after: Fruin proposed one of the earliest approaches to classify congestion in pedestrian crowds (Fruin et al., 1987). Using the Level of Service (LOS) different types of facilities are rated on a scale from A (not crowded) to F (unacceptable overly crowded condition) based on qualitative remarks. Fruin also provides numerical values for density and flow expected at each LOS, but numbers change from facility to facility. The LOS has the advantage of being very practical and since it covers a variety of facilities, it can be considered a versatile definition of congestion levels. In addition, it is constantly updated and it also considers particular cases such as crosswalks (zebra crossings) or escalators (Transportation, 2016). However, the LOS is not universal and an implementation in the frame of real-time crowd control would be difficult. [...] Helbing et al. change_log.after: Direct speed–density evidence is provided by Zhang and Jia (2021): they extend density-only Drake/Greenshields-type relations with a separate conflicting-stream density term. In the extended form, total density alone need not determine walking speed; the conflict parameter controls the extra effect, and setting it to zero recovers the corresponding baseline. Parameters were fitted to speed and density samples extracted from the bidirectional BFR-DML-360 video trajectories. The selected extended linear form fit slightly better than the density-only linear form (reported R² 0.99955 versus 0.99952), and the authors associate the extra opposing-stream effect with lane formation. This is evidence from comparing fitted speed–density models on a bidirectional dataset, not a matched experimental estimate of a universal bidirectional speed penalty. As optional context, Jin et al. report comparable or sometimes higher bidirectional throughput at comparable densities in periodic ring corridors after lane formation. Those flow–density measurements, and the capacity differences summarized by the bidirectional-capacity review, cannot by themselves establish a mean-speed–density difference. The corpus examples therefore need to be reported with their metric, lane organization, geometry and evidence type intact.
change_log.before: The corpus does not support one universal bidirectional speed penalty. Fundamental diagrams differ with directional composition/lane organization and study conditions. Feliciani/Nishinari explicitly discuss distinct uni/bidirectional FD shapes and the limitations of reducing bidirectional dynamics to density and speed alone. In Jin’s periodic corridor experiments, after lane formation the bidirectional flow-density patterns are broadly similar to unidirectional ones; some configurations have higher bidirectional flow at comparable densities due to a low-density fast third lane and the exclusion of a failed lane-formation run. Higher specific flow at the same density implies higher aggregate speed only under matching density/flow definitions, not an independent universally fitted speed curve. The bidirectional-capacity review documents conflicting balanced/unbalanced capacity patterns driven by self-organization and interactions; capacity comparisons alone cannot supply a complete speed-density relation.

basis.anchor_text: The wide-track experiment was performed on Dec. 3, 2016 on a large square. It was a sunny day and there was nearly no wind. The single-file experiment was performed on Dec. 3, 2017, on the same square. The weather was also good. The 278 and 203 student participants in the two experiments, respectively, were recruited through campus advertisements. The age of all of the participants was between 18 and 24, and the male to female ratio was about 1:1. Thus the experimental results are biased toward the behavior of young educated adults. For the wide-track experiment, plastic stools were used to define the boundaries, as shown in Fig. 1(a). The radius of the inner circle was 2 m, and that of the outer circle was 3.5 m. Therefore, the area of the ring corridor was approximately 26 m2.

change_log.after: Merging streams slow and interact near their junction; geometric symmetry, required turning and desired pace affect queues and discharge. The merging-corridor experiment reports more imbalance/clogging in asymmetric deviated branches. The authors suggest accommodating incoming flow by lane changes and upstream stop-and-go propagation as possible explanations, rather than isolated causal tests. Shared downstream space can self-organize into lanes: the experimental review reports a branch-flow lane whose width increment weakens as branch width increases. These observations do not imply an invariant stair/floor half-share. A separate macroscopic node model allocates constrained downstream receiving capacity by equal priorities among currently feasible upstream links, honoring sending limits and turning fractions; this is a model rule, not a measured universal spatial partition. The same corpus review also reports the merging-behavior findings, so its Section 5.8 alone provides a complete secondary-evidence path for both behavior and downstream lane sharing.

This data includes 2338 exit choice samples, in which the attributes of distance, congestion, pedestrian flow to visible exit, pedestrian flow to non-visible exit and exit visibility are considered. Because there are no obstacles in our evacuation scenario, and the exit-choice model does not include visibility parameters, we eliminated the samples that included non-visible exits in the choice set. In this way, the number of observations was reduced to 1503 and 167 decision-makers, including only attributes of distance, pedestrian flow to exits, and congestion. Data were normalized in the range 0–1 to accommodate the parameter estimation to our model requirements.

These choice coefficients are empirically calibrated from individual experimental decisions, with reported estimates for high urgency and uncalibrated defaults separately marked. Lovreglio et al. model the probability of selecting the most crowded exit by random-utility/logit methods using personal/environmental predictors; calibration is stated-choice online survey data, with follow-up interviews probing social influence, not revealed dangerous-evacuation behavior. change_log.after: Bottleneck discharge rates can provide a conditional starting point, not a validated clearance prediction for this station. Liao et al. show that transient and steady-state throughput can differ; a short train-arrival surge need not spend enough time in the regime used to measure capacity. Width alone does not specify initial crowd size, density, behavior or geometry. Li et al. explicitly excluded luggage from their bottleneck trials. Haghani reports luggage-related single-file findings (larger headways, reduced acceleration and a lower-density FD stable point), but these are a review of another study and not a measured luggage correction for this door. Geoerg et al. explicitly leave transfer of assistive-device effects to luggage unresolved. Therefore do not multiply an unrestricted specific flow by 1.2 m and assert that each surge clears. As a dimensional and queueing inference, rather than a formula quoted from Liao, a queue/discharge calculation requires at least passengers per surge, spacing of surges, residual queue and a defensible time-dependent discharge rate for the luggage mix; a constant-rate N/q calculation is only an assumption for a continuously supplied queue and excludes startup/arrival spread. The provided inputs cannot yield a numerical yes/no clearance result. Local matched measurements or a validated calibration would be needed.

change_log.after: Yes. The corpus offers several condition-qualified inputs, not a calibrated evacuation duration for this care home. Fu et al. report corridor speed distributions and speed/flow-density relationships for simulated disabilities and moving helped pairs; they explicitly warn that the participants do not have actual disabilities. Geoerg et al. study real disability/assistance profiles and report bottleneck flows in Table 5 for wheelchair, mixed and reference groups at 0.9 m and 1.2 m widths. The PWD profiles listed in Table 3 span ages 24–61, rather than a representative frail-care-resident cohort; propulsion/assistance mode was not systematically controlled, and the study did not reach the full capacity regime or simulate an emergency. A closer population example appears in Haghani’s review of Kuligowski et al. (2013): 45 residents of a six-storey assisted-living facility were observed in a stair-descent drill, with reported speeds of 0.11–0.29 m/s across self-evacuation, cane use, assistance from another occupant/firefighter and stair-chair use. This is a secondary narrative report, not a walker-only speed or staff-service-time calibration. The same review’s Table 5, however, lists Kuligowski et al. (2013) as 40 evacuees in a classroom, conflicting with that narrative’s sample and venue. That internal discrepancy remains unresolved, so these attributes should be reported as conflicting review descriptions rather than certified primary-study facts. The inclusive social-force model supplies desired-speed, relaxation-time and footprint representations; its described route restrictions are not active in the illustrated single-level case, and guided assistance is not modeled. These data and representations can inform selected movement assumptions, with their original population, geometry and help conditions retained. As an analysis of the target scenario, a numerical duration still requires resident profiles, staff availability and assistance tasks, transfer/pre-movement times and routes. The reviewed paths do not establish a directly transferable staff-roster or walker-specific calibration; this is a limit of these paths, not a verified corpus-wide absence.
change_log.before: Yes, there are usable starting representations and empirical movement data, with important population and assistance limits. Fu et al. provide speed distributions and speed-density/flow-density relationships for corridor counterflow with simulated crutch users, seniors, wheelchair users and blindness; helped participants form moving combinations, and help improves movement efficiency. These participants do not have actual disabilities, so they are not equivalent to care-home residents. Geoerg et al. study actual heterogeneous participants, including manual/electric wheelchair use and personal assistance, and report movement interactions and bottleneck flow. Their mobility profiles are adult volunteers rather than a representative frail older residential-care sample; wheelchair propulsion/assistance was not systematically controlled and capacity conditions were not fully reached. The inclusive social-force model represents disability by desired speed, relaxation time, footprint and navigation rules, but its illustrated simulation has no active helping. These are inputs or model ideas, not a calibrated staff-assisted care-home evacuation time. No walker-specific or staff-roster/service-time calibration has been established by the reviewed sources. Resident mobility/cognition, assistance tasks and staff availability, routes, doors and stairs, pre-movement and transfer times are still needed.

change_log.after: Yes. Opposed-stair and long-descent findings are available, but their conditions must remain separate. Haghani’s review alone provides a complete qualified path: its Table 5 reports a 48-person announced drill in an underwater road tunnel in which upstairs firefighter movement did not negatively affect occupants descending, and a separate up-to-45-person drill in a 20-level building measuring long-stair ascent/descent flow, speed and density. The latter is not stated to be a firefighter-counterflow treatment. The same review also reports a 26-storey residential load study and heterogeneous fatigue-related descent changes. These are secondary reports of distinct studies, not a jointly calibrated 20-storey office/firefighter experiment. Other legitimate paths include a straight-stair bidirectional model, whose original comparison reports lower simulated up- and downstairs speeds than the cited experiment, and real uni-/bidirectional station stair trajectories on a two-flight staircase. They can inform scenario assumptions and sensitivity analysis. None of these selected paths establishes a numeric firefighter-induced slowdown for the hypothetical building. That calculation would require stair geometry, occupant demand/profile, firefighter timing, numbers and equipment, and matched interaction calibration. This does not imply that firefighters universally have no effect.
change_log.before: Yes, there are relevant but separately scoped findings. A straight-stair counterflow personal-space model examines opposed up/down movement, lane formation and deadlock, with a cited experimental comparison; its simulated descent speeds do not fully match experiments. Station staircase trajectories also cover mixed opposing movements on a short facility. Separately, the experimental review covers high-rise ascent/descent, floor-dependent speed/fatigue and long-building drills, including a26-storey residential study. These cover opposing stairs and long descents in different evidence paths, not a jointly calibrated20-storey office/firefighter scenario. They can inform assumptions and sensitivity analysis, but not a defensible numeric slowdown from the given inputs alone. Need stair width/layout, occupant demand/profile, firefighter timing/numbers/equipment and counterflow interaction calibration; model results are not direct firefighter observations.

change_log.after: The corpus offers both observed warning-response associations and a quantitative redirection example, with substantial transfer limits. Van der Wal et al.’s real-incident video analysis found staff guidance associated with less delayed evacuation, while prerecorded/live announcements did not show a significant association with delay in that analysis. Its delayed-response measure concerns the visible majority beginning evacuation and mixes a time threshold with qualitative delaying behaviors; it is not the share of all attendees obeying a message or an individual latency distribution. The analysis is observational and selectively sampled. Separately, Haghani reports Galea et al.’s rail-station drill: an improved active dynamic signage system combined with compatible voice alarm messages redirected 66% of participants to the intended exit; Table 5 describes up to 170 participants. This supplies an actual exit-usage share under the combined intervention, not the isolated causal effect of voice, a phone-notification result or a response-delay distribution. Neither selected example directly calibrates the joint setting of 30,000 outdoor festival attendees and loudspeaker-plus-phone redirection. They can inform what to measure and offer qualified comparison points. A target estimate must distinguish delivery/audibility, phone receipt, comprehension, acceptance and physical movement, and use matched response data and congestion constraints; 66% must not be assigned to this festival.
change_log.before: The reviewed research offers qualitative guidance, but not a calibrated share-and-delay estimate for this festival. In real-incident video analysis, staff guidance was associated with less delayed evacuation; prerecorded and live announcements did not show a significant relationship with delayed response in that analysis. Its measure concerns the majority of visible people beginning evacuation, not the proportion of all attendees complying with a congestion-redirection message. The study is correlational, selectively sampled and incomplete off-camera. Its communication categories include alarms, staff guidance, prerecorded messages and live announcements, rather than a tested loudspeaker-plus-phone notification intervention. Thus it can motivate clear, situation-specific guidance and local measurement, but supplies neither a defensible compliance percentage nor a latency distribution for 30,000 outdoor festival attendees. Message delivery/audibility, phone receipt, comprehension, acceptance and actual movement must be distinguished; target-channel response data and local congestion constraints would be needed.

change_log.after: The corpus includes unidirectional, nearly balanced bidirectional and explicitly unbalanced counterflow configurations. Jin et al.’s ring-road runs switch from one direction to nearly balanced opposing participant numbers; their Eq. (2) defines local specific flow as crossings divided by width and observation time. A more directly relevant alternative is Hänseler et al.’s analysis of Hong Kong counterflow experiments: a 3 m by 9 m corridor at 180 degrees, with group-size ratios approximately 10:0, 9:1, 8:2, 7:3, 6:4 and 5:5. The experiments lasted about one minute with one run per configuration. Their stream-based density-speed model was calibrated on experiments #85 and #87 and checked against #84, #86, #88 and #89, retaining distinct directions, densities and speeds. Participant group-size ratios must not automatically be equated to an instantaneous cross-section flow split. The corpus capacity synthesis also reports conflicting balanced/unbalanced capacity patterns and lane-organization effects. These are legitimate comparison/calibration materials for a majority/minority case, not a universal bridge flow-per-metre capacity. As dimensional reasoning, dividing demand by specific flow yields a conditional width only when total versus per-direction flow, units, split, operating density and effective geometry match. A density-speed curve is not itself a flow-per-width number. The actual peak demand, minority share and target operating conditions remain necessary for a numerical width; a measured maximum need not be a suitable operating value.
change_log.before: The reviewed corpus contains single-direction diagrams and bidirectional diagrams whose directional composition must be retained. Jin et al. measured unidirectional ring-road runs followed by opposite-direction runs with nearly balanced participant numbers, as Table A.1 confirms; these are not a measured majority-to-minority post-event split. The bidirectional capacity synthesis explicitly compares balanced, unbalanced and unidirectional configurations, reporting conflicting U/W-shaped capacity–flow-ratio relationships and important effects of lane organization and experimental instructions. Thus the presence of some reverse walkers cannot be handled by treating a balanced or unidirectional curve as a universal per-metre capacity. Dividing total peak demand by a specific total flow can give a conditional dimensional width calculation only if demand and the selected value use compatible units, the actual directional split, density/regime, lane organization and effective geometry. A per-direction flow must not be confused with the total of both directions. These studies provide comparison/calibration material; the unspecified minority share, actual demand, bridge constraints and transferable operating flow are still needed for a numerical width. A measured maximum capacity alone does not establish an acceptable operating condition.

change_log.after: Yes, at least one implemented corpus model explicitly represents familiarity, but its empirical setting is only a limited analogue for the mall. Wu et al. model facility-layout familiarity through which exits a pedestrian knows and through different potential-field calculations for familiar and unfamiliar pedestrians. Their exit-choice logit normalizes over known exits; familiar pedestrians are assumed to know all exits, while unfamiliar pedestrians know some through guide signs. A familiar-population share φ and an expectation weight θ for hidden-route conditions enter the model. This is facility knowledge and anticipated route conditions, not an independently fitted habit preference for a previously used main door over an equally known side door. The empirical case is normal leaving at Beijing’s Zhichun Road subway station: 481 pedestrians choose the directly visible stairway (Exit 2) or continue towards the escalator (Exit 1). Immediate choosers are described as possibly familiar, while hesitation and reselection supply the other behavioral classes. Familiarity was inferred from observed choice behavior, rather than independently measured prior experience. The authors impose observed entrance flow and the inferred familiarity composition in simulations, tune a parameter against stair choices and fit θ against observed stairway flows, with a within-setting consistency check. These are genuine empirical calibration steps, but they do not validate emergency shopping-mall main/side-exit shares. Optional contrasts remain useful: the boundedly rational model assumes everyone knows the scenario, and CellEVAC’s chosen utility/persistence attributes do not encode prior familiarity and were optimized rather than fitted to real/survey data. A mall application would need measured exit awareness or prior use, visibility/signage, relative route disutilities and matched calibration. No station stair-choice percentage should be relabelled as a mall side-exit prediction, and the old negative examples cannot establish that familiarity-sensitive models are absent from the corpus.
change_log.before: The existing evidence supports the following selected-model findings, but the overall corpus-level question remains unresolved. Familiarity is recognized in corpus route-choice research, but recognition in a literature discussion must not be confused with a fitted familiarity parameter. The route-choice principles synthesis describes preference for known exits and incomplete knowledge of alternatives in emergencies. In the boundedly rational model, all evacuees are explicitly assumed familiar with the scenario, and wayfinding is omitted: it cannot represent the stated difference in exit knowledge without extending and testing that assumption. CellEVAC mentions familiarity among possible influences, but its selected utility attributes are distance, width, route group size, exit congestion, current-choice persistence and system guidance; persistence is not prior familiarity. Its stated purpose was optimization rather than calibration with real or survey data. These reviewed implementations therefore do not establish a side-exit percentage for mall visitors with asymmetric familiarity. The corpus offers mechanisms and model choices to examine, but the analyst needs exit-awareness/familiarity observations, relative distances/queues, visibility and guidance, and calibration/validation in a comparable population/layout. The conclusion concerns these reviewed models; it is not a claim that no corpus model ever encodes familiarity. A complete check of candidate familiarity-sensitive implementations and their calibration is still required; these negative examples do not establish that none exists in the corpus.

initial_review.proposed_revision_reference_answer:
Yes, some corpus models represent familiarity-related exit knowledge, although this should not be confused with a fitted preference for a previously used door. Wu et al., ‘Simulation of pedestrian route choice with local view’ (pearl-src-96b26d7574a0faec, PDF pp. 6 and 16), limits each pedestrian’s logit choice set to known exits and uses different potential-field algorithms for familiar and unfamiliar pedestrians; phi sets the familiar fraction. Familiar pedestrians know the facility’s exits, whereas unfamiliar pedestrians obtain partial exit knowledge from signs. By contrast, the reviewed boundedly rational model assumes everyone already knows the scenario (pearl-src-e51fb7757831d3bc, p. 2), and CellEVAC’s six-attribute utility has current-choice persistence rather than prior exit familiarity and was optimized rather than calibrated with real or survey choices (pearl-src-a1d94e43220548c2, pp. 6–7).

Wu et al. developed and calibrated their model using normal egress observations of 481 people at a Beijing subway station choosing between stairs and an escalator (PDF pp. 3–4, 21–22). This is a useful partial comparison: two alternatives, incomplete visibility, and pedestrians with different inferred layout knowledge. It differs from the mall’s within-person main-entrance/side-exit familiarity asymmetry, from emergency evacuation, and from two otherwise comparable doors; familiarity classes were inferred from behavior. Thus the corpus contains a relevant familiarity-sensitive mechanism and a partly comparable empirical calibration, but this path does not establish a transferable mall side-exit share or a separately identified prior-door-familiarity effect. Use the model as a candidate requiring mall-specific exit-awareness, visibility, route/queue data and validation. This is a limitation of the demonstrated path, not a verified claim that no exact corpus match exists.

change_log.after: Yes, there is directly relevant right-angle crowded cross-flow evidence, though it is not a ready-made station delay penalty. Hänseler et al. use a TU Berlin entrance-hall crossing at roughly 90 degrees, with a reported maximum density of 5 persons/m² and mainly student pedestrians. They model and compare route-specific walking-time distributions, explicitly including interactions between streams. Table 5 reports observed route-mean walking times of 12.4 s on the 9 m major W→E route (118 observations) and 10.6 s on the approximately 7 m minor N→SE/SW route (46 observations). These are total route times under that crossing configuration, not time added by crossing relative to a matched non-crossing baseline. The anisotropic stream-based model better captures route differences, but the crossing case parameters were calibrated on the full data set and residual individual variability is substantial. This provides usable model/data structure for estimating each stream once local geometry, inflows, densities, composition and a baseline are supplied; peak hour alone is not a numerical density specification. No fixed additional seconds can be transferred to the hypothetical hall.

change_log.after: The corpus has decision-relevant outcomes, but matching exit width alone is insufficient. Chen et al. used a 1 m exit with 97 mainly university-student participants and double S-shaped guardrails, comparing with no obstacles. They measured exit timing/headways/flow and spatial density; rails prolonged evacuation while limiting maximum area density. These are not a single column or a demonstrated 500-person hall result. Zanlungo et al. show repeated bottleneck drills with and without a round obstacle at a 0.75 m exit; density and congestion-number maxima move to the obstacle sides, and density and unstable-motion maxima need not coincide. This bears on where crowding occurs but is not an outflow improvement estimate. Haghani’s secondary synthesis reports mixed findings for columns/panels: its human laboratory rows report effects of size, distance and exit location on outflow, as well as pressure relief without a change in total evacuation time. Its animal/insect rows must be distinguished from direct human evidence. The operator should compare obstacle-free and specified column placement using both outflow and local crowding measures. The proposed column diameter, setback/lateral gap and crowd conditions are unspecified, and the reviewed examples do not establish their effect at the joint 1 m/500-person setting. No universal beneficial-column conclusion follows.
change_log.before: The corpus has decision-relevant outcomes, but matching exit width alone is insufficient. Zanlungo et al. show repeated bottleneck drills with and without a round obstacle at a 0.75 m exit; density and congestion-number maxima move to the obstacle sides, and density and unstable-motion maxima need not coincide. This bears on where crowding occurs but is not an outflow improvement estimate. Haghani’s empirical synthesis reports mixed findings for columns/panels: size, distance and exit location matter; pressure can improve without changing total evacuation time. The operator should compare obstacle-free and specified column placement using both outflow and local crowding measures. The proposed column diameter, setback/lateral gap and crowd conditions are unspecified, and the reviewed examples do not establish their effect at the joint 1 m/500-person setting. initial_review.question: A venue operator is deciding whether to place a column-like obstacle in front of the single 1 m wide exit of a hypothetical hall holding 500 people. change_log.after: The corpus offers limited real/virtual correspondence through two useful paths. Van Beek et al. compare ordinary wayfinding in a real multi-storey university building with matched immersive-VR assignments: same-floor strategy similarity coexists with absolute between-floor differences and differences in head angular speed. The interface also constrains locomotion, so time differences alone do not establish invalidity. These were individual wayfinding tasks with no other people present, not a crowded evacuation. Table 1 reports real-life familiarity responses but no VR familiarity values, and the authors did not test familiarity effects; the body text’s final “unknown” sentence has an ambiguous group referent. A more evacuation-focused alternative is Li et al. (2025): 48 college students used a 2D multi-person mouse-controlled virtual platform, and door-use shares were compared with a previous controlled field experiment in matching scenarios. The paper reports close route-choice correspondence, illustrated by Fig. 5. However, participants were first told the door, obstacle and exit locations in the learning scenario S0. This is useful route-choice evidence with interface/training limits, not validation for visitors who do not know a hospital wing. Haghani’s review also reports qualitative field/VR route-choice agreement, as a secondary statement rather than a new independent test. Neither selected validation path by itself establishes unfamiliar-hospital signage predictions. Matching tasks, sign visibility, interface and prior knowledge, and testing relevant real-building choices with unfamiliar visitors, would be sensible target-validation steps. Do not conclude that all VR route choices are validated or invalid.
change_log.before: The corpus offers direct real-versus-immersive-VR wayfinding validation, with qualified rather than universal correspondence. Van Beek et al. compare matched assignments in a real multi-story university building and its virtual replica. Single-floor wayfinding strategies were similar, while between-floor tasks showed relative similarity but absolute differences; head angular speeds also differed. Travel-time differences alone do not prove VR behavior invalid because the VR locomotion settings constrained speed. This supports using VR for some design comparisons while checking the particular task and interface. It does not establish that evacuation-sign placement results transfer unchanged to unfamiliar hospital visitors: the tasks were wayfinding in a university building, with no other people present, not a crowded hospital emergency. The field sample was described as mostly somewhat/very familiar with the building, familiarity effects were not analyzed, and familiarity of the comparison participants is reported as unknown. Therefore unfamiliarity-specific validity was not demonstrated. For the hospital use, match layout, sign legibility and viewing/locomotion conditions, recruit unfamiliar visitors and compare relevant real-building choices/sign detection before turning VR preferences into placement predictions. Do not conclude that all VR route choices are invalid or all are validated.

change_log.after: As shown in Fig. 8, the flows in the three experiments are all linearly dependent on bottleneck width. We choose a linear regression y = k · x (see Eq. (2)). Since Js = ρ · v, the specific flow concept gives J = Js · W. Here W is the bottleneck width b. Note that bottleneck width b = 0.4 m is the minimum width for pedestrians to pass. Thus, the regression line for b smaller than 0.4 m has no physical meaning with respect to pedestrian flow. The fitting degree is evaluated by the coefficient of determination R2 (see Appendix C), which ranges from 0 to 1. The linearity fits the best when R2 = 1. In Fig. 8 all the values of R2 are above 0.880 (see Table C.1), which indicates that the linearity is relatively reliable. This reconfirms that the specific flow is constant as bottleneck width changes [2,4].

change_log.after: The corpus supports a conditional linear approximation over tested settings, not a universal flow-width law. Liao et al. reanalyze cooperative, purposeful walking without haste: EG tested ten widths from 0.9 to 2.5 m, AO five from 2.4 to 5.0 m, and UO three sets spanning 0.7 to 2.0 m. These are discrete settings, not continuous exhaustive validation. Their fitted flow-width relations are linear within these groups, but the slopes can change between all-state and steady-state selection. The experiments also differ in geometry. Nicolas et al. summarize earlier evidence for approximate proportional scaling and a stepwise alternative based on only two widths; that is secondary discussion, not an additional independently verified experiment here. Li et al. tested able-bodied, luggage-free adults instructed to run as if there were a fire, in a 45-degree funnel with widths 0.60–1.65 m in 0.15-m steps. Their results paragraph reports increasing specific flow with increasing width for running, in contrast to the approximately constant specific flow discussed for ordinary walking. This comparison spans different treatments and geometries and does not isolate a universal causal geometry effect. Geoerg et al. explicitly limit their heterogeneous-crowd experiment to free-flow conditions below 3 persons/m² that do not reach geometric capacity, with emergency transfer untested. A defensible linear approximation must therefore retain the tested geometry, population, behavioral regime and averaging window; these examples do not establish one transferable slope outside those conditions.
change_log.before: There is support for a conditional linear approximation, not a universal law over all widths or populations. Liao et al. reanalyze cooperative purposeful walking without haste in three groups: EG widths 0.9-2.5 m (ten settings), AO 2.4-5.0 m (five settings), and UO several sets spanning 0.7-2.0 m. They report linear flow-width fits and approximately constant specific flow within these tests, while all-state and steady-state slopes can differ. The three groups also differ in bottleneck length and approach geometry. Nicolas et al. describe approximate proportional scaling as condition-dependent and discuss a stepwise alternative based on limited two-width evidence. Li et al. examine running able-bodied, luggage-free adults through a 45-degree funnel with widths 0.60-1.65 m in 0.15-m steps; their specific-flow behavior differs from ordinary walking, and geometry matters. Geoerg et al. include wheelchair/heterogeneous crowds at limited widths and explicitly warn that their free-flow conditions do not reach geometric capacity. Thus neither a single transferable slope nor extrapolation to very narrow openings, haste/pushing, luggage or assisted crowds follows from this corpus. A linear fit should retain its tested geometry, population, behavioral regime and averaging window.

change_log.after: internal validity of a crowd experiment refers to the extent to which the experiment can reveal genuine causal relations (or the extent to which it can reveal the absence of causal relationship). Maximising this feature of a crowd experiment could often necessitate abstraction, simplification and exertion of high levels of experimental control. External validity of a crowd experiment, on the other hand, concerns the extent of generalisability of findings to the contexts beyond the experiment setting. Often, these two features of a crowd experiment could conflict and create a trade-off. This conflict and its implications on experiment design as well as interpretation and assessment of experimental findings in crowd dynamics essentially constitutes the main motivation of this work. Enhancing external validity of experiments often can only come at the cost of compromising internal validity and losing experimental control, and vice versa. In other words, in vast majority of cases, the investigator cannot maintain high levels of both dimensions at the same time. The more the investigator controls for extraneous factors, the more he/she relinquishes the ability to generalise the findings to a broader context. Therefore, it would be essential to consciously recognise the dimension of validity (i.e., internal or external) that matters the most to each investigation and tailor the design of the experiment accordingly.

change_log.after: When the crowd size is small, the addition of an S-shaped guardrail will prolong the evacuation time. Software ‘Tracker’ was used to extract data such as that on the pedestrian track in videos of the experiment. after.anchor_text: In our experiments, we explored whether certain strategies could be implemented by social groups to enhance system efficiency. We tested two strategies: handholding and line formation. The handholding strategy produced variable effects that were mostly statistically insig- nificant, whereas the line formation strategy significantly and consis- tently improved system efficiency. Remarkably, adopting the line formation strategy reduced the total evacuation time to levels even lower than those observed in crowds composed solely of solo individuals in some cases. The overall improvement was consistent across both small and larger group sizes.
after.conditions: Handholding had mostly statistically insignificant effects; line formation reduced system evacuation time in tested groups; no measured injury reduction.

change_log.after: The corpus-wide predominant method remains unresolved in this revision: the 106-source method ledger is not yet a fully adjudicated, deduplicated study census. The verified intervention evidence contains several distinct methods. Zhang and Jia's inflow control, CellEVAC/leader-following guidance and distance-keeping MPC are evaluated in computer simulations. Empirical model calibration does not establish field effectiveness, and the MPC paper's Deployment environment is itself a simulator; the related prediction-model paper leaves real-crowd controller testing to future work. Controlled human evidence is substantial enough that it must be represented explicitly. Chen's 97-volunteer guardrail experiment found longer evacuation time for the small crowd and maximum area density no greater than without obstacles. Yi's 17-person experiment tested queueing instructions, with a separate model-based extension. Haghani and Yazdani recruited 120 people, tested subgroups of 60 and found mostly insignificant handholding effects but consistent clearance-time improvement from line formation under the tested conditions and full compliance. Bode and colleagues reanalysed two days of human crossing experiments: roundabout instructions and a central column changed some movement patterns but did not change facility capacity. The Love Parade paper provides qualitative real-event reconstruction rather than a controlled intervention-effect estimate. These results support intervention-, geometry-, demand- and compliance-specific statements about simulated or measured flow, density, order and evacuation performance. They do not by themselves establish general injury-risk reductions; the leader-guidance paper explicitly limits its pressure-based safety measure to comparison rather than precise accident probability. A field-versus-simulation majority, a robust change in that majority under broader inclusion, and a corpus-wide staged-release gap are not asserted while eligibility, research batches and shared-data/model lineages remain unresolved.
change_log.before: In the cases checked, Zhang and Jia assess feedback inflow control by simulation, even though their speed–density relationship is compared with real-world data. The MPC prediction-model paper estimates models from microscopic simulation data and calls real-crowd testing future work. The Love Parade paper supplies a qualitative reconstruction from public videos and materials, not a controlled causal effectiveness estimate. Additional checked cases include simulated CellEVAC/leader–follower guidance and distance-keeping MPC; the latter's “Deployment environment” is still a pedestrian simulator. Chen et al. conducted a 97-volunteer controlled experiment with S-shaped guardrails and a no-obstacle comparison: evacuation time was prolonged while maximum area density was reduced. This is human experimental evidence, not a deployed emergency injury-prevention trial. These case-specific findings support distinctions between model-based benefits, controlled human measurements and real-event reconstruction, and between density/flow proxies and injury outcomes. They do not determine the corpus-wide predominant method. Eligible studies, scope-boundary cases and cross-publication study identities are not completely resolved, so no field-versus-simulation majority or overall method proportion is asserted. Confidence must remain tied to each study's intervention, demand, compliance, geometry, endpoint and validation level; general injury-risk reductions and staged-release causal effects are not established by the checked cases.
change_log.reason: Correct Chen’s result and represent newly verified human interventions without asserting an unverified majority.

change_log.after: However, it is important to remark that real measurements of pedestrian properties result in a number of dots dispersed over a large surface roughly defining the behavior indicated as a line in Fig 1. Therefore, clearly determining if a given flow configuration has to be considered congested may become difficult by using the FD alone. For example, Zhang et al. [19] found that fundamental diagrams for unidirectional and bidirectional flow are different. In addition, while the definition of capacity and critical density appears as a single and unique point in the representation of Fig 1, in reality, transition to congestion occurs at a range of densities. In brief, capacity is a rather simple definition from a theoretical perspective, but defining it in practical terms becomes much more difficult. As we will see in the next section, for the bidirectional case considered here the flow ratio plays a central role when investigating the transition to congestion. [...] Finally, it should be also noted that, in the case of simulation, the deadlock concept is very often used. Some authors used simulations to study the density at which the “jamming transition” occurs, i.e. the density at which deadlocks occur and pedestrians cannot cross the corridor at all. Although this type of studies are important to develop better simulation models, the relation with reality is uncertain since deadlocks almost never occur in real situations and a minimal flow was reported also under very extreme conditions [18, 20, 21] (the origin and nature of this minimum flow is not clear). Therefore, although we will often refer to deadlock occurrence as a phase transition while reviewing simulation models, it is important to remind that this concept do not necessarily applies to real situations

after.anchor_text: At high densities, the velocities are very low and thus the errors in the measurements are usually not small. Therefore, following Guo et al. (2016), we used a traditional area-based method to measure the densities and the cross-section method to measure the flow rate. Fig. 4 shows the fundamental diagrams for both experiments. Two different coordination systems were used. The wide-track experimental results correspond to the bottom and left coordinate axis. The single-file experimental results correspond to the top and right coordinate axis. We averaged the local measure results over the density interval of 0.2 ped/m2 for the wide-track experiment and 0.2 ped/m for the single-file experiment. Here we also show the raw data before averaging for the wide-track experiment in Fig. 4(b), and the wide-scattered appearance could be clearly found. [transcription: In the wide-track experiment, ρc1 ≈ 2.5 ped/m² marks the maximum specific flow of about 1.7 ped/(m·s). The decreasing branches are similar below ρc2 ≈ 6 ped/m² in the wide-track experiment and ρ′c2 ≈ 2.5 ped/m in the single-file experiment.]
after.conditions: Unidirectional ring-track and single-file experiments; area-based density and cross-section flow; wide-track means binned at 0.2 ped/m². Values are source-reported approximate markers, not visually estimated jam thresholds.

change_log.after: The evidence supports condition-specific operational markers, but these must not be relabeled as one measurement-independent density at which pedestrian flow becomes unstable or jammed. The bidirectional-capacity synthesis distinguishes the fundamental-diagram maximum (critical/capacity density) from a theoretical zero-flow jam density and notes that observed transition is spread over a density range. Jin et al.'s wide-track experiment reports a capacity peak near 2.5 ped/m² and a separate body-contact transition near 6 ped/m². The latter accompanies a change in the decreasing-flow branch; it is not an observed universal standstill or stop-and-go onset. In that 1.5 m wide-track unidirectional setting typical stop-and-go waves did not emerge, whereas the single-file experiment showed them in an intermediate-density regime. The same paper cites prior method comparisons with similar averaged values but different standard deviations; this is secondary support for mean comparability, not an onset test. Measurement robustness is also conditional: the follow-up ring-corridor analysis reports consistent statistics for 6–10 subareas and 10–20 s intervals. That is positive evidence for those processing choices, not invariance to every density estimator or validation of a jam-onset number. Nicolas et al. summarize prior spatial/temporal averaging differences, and Liao's direct bottleneck reanalysis shows that all-state and steady-state flow estimates differ. The ring-corridor authors also explicitly distinguish flow-rate fluctuations from stop-and-go waves and leave quantitative stability across densities for further testing. Force-based-model stability analysis adds a separate warning: mathematically unstable regimes can produce backward motion and overlap instead of realistic jams. Thus any claimed threshold must specify its physical endpoint, geometry, direction mix, density convention, averaging and stationarity definition. The reviewed evidence does not turn the reported 2.5 or 6 ped/m² markers into a method-robust instability or jamming trigger.
change_log.before: The corpus supports identifying an operational, condition-specific transition or fitted critical density, but the reviewed evidence does not justify one universal method-robust density for instability or jamming. The capacity synthesis defines FD critical density at maximum flow, distinguishes the theoretical zero-flow jam density, and notes that measured transition occupies a range and that simulated deadlocks do not necessarily describe real pedestrian flow. Organized lanes can still become congested, so loss of organization, capacity and standstill are different criteria. Measurement also matters: Nicolas et al. discuss different spatial/temporal averaging giving different flow/density results, especially at high density. Liao et al. demonstrate that all-run and steady-state-selected bottleneck flows can differ significantly, with measurement regions and state selection explicitly defined. These findings require stating the instability definition, geometry/direction mix, population, local versus global density, averaging and stationary interval before estimating a threshold. A threshold can be compared across methods only on the same trajectories/conditions with uncertainty; a fitted jam-density parameter or FD maximum is not by itself a validated instability trigger. No common numerical value is asserted here.

change_log.after: Lane formation is represented by several operational observables. In the bidirectional-capacity study, cells with the same x-velocity direction define lanes, empty cells are ignored, and the lane-count mean and variation are measured along the corridor. Those counts alone can misclassify a chessboard-like configuration. The study therefore also defines row-wise direction segregation, its global average Φ, and a composite disorganization measure Var(Nlanes)/(Avg(Nlanes)·Φ). The random baseline for Φ depends on the flow ratio and the number of grid columns, so the same raw Φ is not automatically comparable across configurations. This study uses several supervised datasets with similar acquisition/geometrical arrangements but different experimental procedures. As another example, Jin et al. use the direction-specific mean and sample standard deviation of radial positions in a ring corridor; stabilization of those series, interpreted with snapshots, marks the lane-formation process and its duration TLF. This is a different observable and geometry, and the cited passage does not specify a universal numerical tolerance for stabilization. These measures can be used as model-validation targets if experiment and model share the definition, trajectory processing, spatial grid or radial convention, observation window, geometry, density and directional/instruction conditions. That is a conditional validation recommendation inferred from the operational definitions and their stated limitations, not evidence that one interchangeable lane scalar validates every counterflow scenario.
change_log.before: Lane formation has been quantified in several operationally different ways. Jin et al. track the direction-specific mean and standard deviation of radial positions in a ring corridor: stabilization of these series, interpreted with snapshots, identifies lane formation and its duration; different final lane counts and multi-stage transitions are distinguished. The bidirectional-capacity study uses a gridded velocity field: contiguous same-direction cells define lanes, yielding their mean number and spatial variation; a row-wise direction-segregation order parameter and a combined disorganization measure supplement lane counts. It explicitly notes that lane counts alone can misclassify organization and that the order parameter depends on directional ratio and a nonzero random baseline. These are useful validation observables when the same trajectory processing and experiment geometry/density/directional split/instructions are reproduced. They are not interchangeable scalar thresholds: ring radii versus straight-corridor grid rows, counting conventions, resolution and temporal selection differ. A counterflow model can be evaluated against lane count, formation-time distributions and organization dynamics using a matched definition, preferably alongside flow/speed data. Merely producing visually recognizable lanes or matching an unmatched order parameter does not establish model validity across studies.

change_log.after: Yes, the corpus contains reports of a faster-is-slower effect, but the provenance and conditions matter. Haghani's empirical review lists positive laboratory-human evidence, including Garcimartín et al. (2014), and reports Pastor et al.'s findings for humans, sheep and grains. Those are secondary reports in a corpus review, not primary verification here of every cited experiment; Table 5 is not a set of independent replications. The same table includes mixed or contrary laboratory results: effects depending on the number of participants, shorter discharge when rushing involves no dangerous pressure or explicit aggressive pushing, and faster-is-faster under slow running. The review explains that competition/aggression differences can account for apparently opposing findings, and explicitly excludes numerical studies from that table comparison. A direct corpus experiment by Nicolas et al., using a 72-cm door, polite/selfish instructions and placid/hurried walkers, found higher global flow with more selfish or hurried participants. It excluded extreme panic, violence, high pressure and extreme haste; extrapolation to extreme emergencies remains unresolved. Separately, Maity et al. interpret their numerical AR/PW/ARZ comparison as FIS: AR has higher speed than its equilibrium relation in dense regions yet the longest overall evacuation time. This is numerical, cross-model evidence and does not isolate the effect of increasing desired speed or pushing within one unchanged model. Thus the reviewed evidence supports conditional occurrences, not a rule that any increase in walking speed must reduce outflow. Report the evidence type, behavioral/contact treatment, geometry and outcome; whole-evacuation time and local outflow should not be conflated.
change_log.before: Yes, the corpus contains faster-is-slower evidence, but of several distinct kinds and with limits. Haghani’s empirical synthesis explicitly lists positive human-laboratory bottleneck studies as well as animal/insect/frictional-particle evidence; it also lists contrary or conditional human results. Its human examples distinguish stronger competitive/contact behavior from mere urgency or slow running: nonaggressive rushing need not prolong discharge. Nicolas et al. provide a direct limited-pushing human counterexample, finding increased global flow with more selfish/hurried walking and explicitly leaving extrapolation to extreme emergencies unresolved. Simulations also produce analogous phenomena: Maity et al.’s obstructed-corridor comparison associates the AR model’s higher high-density speed with longer evacuation than the alternative models. That is model-based evidence under those equations/configuration, not observation of actual panic or a pure measured human dose-response. Therefore stronger drive can reduce discharge in some constricted competitive/contact regimes, but the corpus does not support a universal rule that faster walking always reduces flow. State the human/animal/model evidence type, bottleneck layout, contact/competition, density, treatment and outcome definition; evacuation time and instantaneous outflow are related but not interchangeable without accounting for arrivals and population.

The bidirectional-capacity analysis states that PeTrack can achieve positional accuracy up to 1 cm depending on cameras and markers; this is a conditional capability statement, not a measured error distribution for every trajectory. Consequently one can assess relative credibility and processing conventions, but cannot assign all reported speed/density values a universal precision from a software accuracy claim.
